The days are dog-eared, the edges torn, ragged—like those pages I ripped once out of library books, for their photos of Vallejo and bootless Robert Johnson. A fine needs paying now it’s true, but not by me. I am no more guilty than that thrush is who sits there stripping moss off the wet bark of a tree. A red fleck, like his, glows at the back of my head—a beauty mark, left by the brain’s after-jets. I would not wish for the three brains Robert required to double-clutch his guitar and chase those sounds he had to know led down and into a troubled dusky river, always. Three brains did Johnson no earthly good, neither his nor Vallejo’s 4 & 1/2 worked right exactly—O bunglers, O banged-up pans of disaster! Crying for days, said Cesar, & singing for months. How can I be so strong some times, at others weak? I wish to be free, but free to do what? To leave myself behind? To switch channels remotely? Better to sing. Not like the bird, but as they sang, Cesar & Robert— with the shocked & seeded sweetness of an apple split open by a meat cleaver.

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version:

---

The days are dog-eared, their edges torn and ragged—like those pages I once ripped from library books, coveting their photographs of Vallejo and bootless Robert Johnson. A fine must be paid now, it's true, but not by me. I am no more guilty than that thrush who sits there stripping moss from the wet bark of a tree. A red fleck, like his, glows at the back of my head—a beauty mark, left by the brain's after-jets. I would not wish for the three brains Robert required to double-clutch his guitar and chase those sounds he surely knew led down and into a troubled, dusky river, always. Three brains did Johnson no earthly good; neither his nor Vallejo's four-and-a-half worked quite right—O bunglers, O banged-up pans of disaster! Crying for days, said Cesar, and singing for months. How can I be so strong at some times, so weak at others? I wish to be free—but free to do what? To leave myself behind? To switch channels remotely? Better to sing. Not like the bird, but as they sang, Cesar and Robert—with the shocked and seeded sweetness of an apple split open by a meat cleaver.

---

**Notes on the revisions:** I preserved the poem's distinctive voice, imagery, and rhythm while refining a few phrasings for flow and clarity: "coveting their photographs" adds precision to the act of tearing out pages; "he surely knew" reads more naturally than "he had to know"; "four-and-a-half" spells out the numeral for a more literary register; and "How can I be so strong at some times, so weak at others?" balances the parallel structure more gracefully. All original imagery and meaning remain intact.
outputs.L2: The days have worn thin, their corners bent and frayed—much like the pages I once tore from library books to steal their images of Vallejo and Robert Johnson without his shoes. Someone owes a penalty now, that much is certain, but the debt isn't mine to settle. My innocence matches that of the thrush perched over there, peeling moss from the damp bark of a tree. At the base of my skull burns a crimson spot, just like his—a mark of beauty scorched there by the mind's exhaust. I'd never covet the trio of brains that Johnson supposedly possessed to work his guitar's clutch and pursue those melodies he surely understood would carry him downward, forever into some shadowed, restless river. But those three brains brought him no salvation on this earth, and neither his nor Vallejo's four-and-a-half functioned properly—oh, what clumsy souls, what battered vessels of ruin! Weeping for days, Cesar told us, and singing for months. Why does such power surge through me one moment, only to abandon me the next? Freedom is what I long for—but freedom aimed at what? To abandon my own self? To change the station from afar? Singing serves me better. Not in the manner of that bird, but the way those two men sang, Cesar and Robert—carrying the startled, seed-bearing sweetness of an apple cloven in two by a butcher's blade.

**Torn Pages**

My days feel worn and damaged, frayed at the edges like something handled too roughly and too often. They remind me of pages torn from library books—those small acts of theft I committed to steal photographs of Vallejo and Robert Johnson, faces I could not bear to leave behind on the shelf. There was something in me that needed them near, even if possessing them meant ruining the very volumes that held them. My days carry that same quality of damage: something taken, something spoiled, something loved beyond the bounds of what was permitted.

Yet I refuse to accept the guilt for this, or for any debt they say I owe. My innocence is not the polished innocence of one who has never touched the world, but the fierce, instinctive innocence of a thrush stripping moss from the bark of a tree. The bird does not apologize for its hunger; it takes what it needs to build and to survive, and no one calls it a thief. So it is with me. I will not bow my head to a ledger I never agreed to, nor confess to crimes that are only the natural motions of a life reaching for what sustains it.

And how could I not reach? When I consider the extraordinary genius of Robert Johnson and Cesar Vallejo, I am struck silent with wonder. They possessed gifts so rare that they seem almost impossible—voices and visions that pierced straight through the ordinary surface of things. But here is the cruel arithmetic of their lives: those very gifts brought them suffering rather than any earthly reward. Vallejo died poor and far from home; Johnson died young and haunted, his brilliance leaving him no safer, no richer, no more at peace. Their genius was not a shield but an open wound, and the world took far more from them than it ever gave.

Knowing this, I wrestle with my own contradictions. I swing between strength and weakness like a door left open in the wind, certain one moment that I can endure anything, undone the next by the smallest sorrow. I ask myself what freedom would even mean—whether it is the power to escape my circumstances, or simply the willingness to stop fighting my own nature. I cannot answer. The question turns over and over in me, offering no rest, only the restless motion of a mind that will not settle.

But in the end I make my choice. I will not try to escape myself, to flee from the person I am into some safer, quieter life. Instead, I will sing—sing with the raw and shocking sweetness that Vallejo and Johnson embodied, the kind of sweetness that startles because it comes at such cost. I want to open myself the way an apple is split open by a cleaver: cleanly, suddenly, the pale flesh exposed all at once to the light. Let it hurt. Let it be sweet. Let it be true. That is the only freedom I can imagine worth having.
outputs.L4:
# On Singing from the Wound

The poem opens in a place of unrest, where the speaker finds himself drawn irresistibly toward the company of artists who suffered for their vision. He thinks of Cesar Vallejo, the Peruvian poet who wrote of dying in Paris on a rainy day, whose verses seemed to bleed with a peculiar and unbearable tenderness. He thinks too of Robert Johnson, the bluesman said to have bargained his soul at the crossroads, whose voice cracked open with a sound too raw to be merely performed. These figures are not distant heroes to be admired from afar; the speaker identifies with them, feeling their torment echo in his own restless heart.

The imagery moves in fragments, refusing the comfort of a smooth narrative. Broken pictures surface and dissolve—a hand, a rain-slicked street, the neck of a guitar, a mouth open in song or in grief. This fracturing is not carelessness but design, for the poem enacts the very brokenness it describes. The speaker interrupts himself with questions, turning inward with a relentless self-interrogation: *What have I done? Why am I so weak? What have I earned that I should be forgiven?* Guilt threads through these lines like a low current, the guilt of one who feels unworthy of the gift he carries, or unworthy of the pain that seems to accompany it.

To make sense of this suffering, the speaker reaches toward the natural world. He measures himself against the patience of trees, the indifferent flow of rivers, the way birds sing without apparent reason or reward. Nature offers a mirror and a rebuke: it endures, it continues, it releases its sound into the air without self-consciousness. The speaker longs for that same freedom—to be released from the burden of his weakness, to shed the weight of his guilt, to move through the world as unencumbered as wind through leaves. Yet he knows he is not a tree or a river. He is a human being, fragile and self-aware, caught between his aspiration and his frailty.

It is precisely in facing this fragility that the poem arrives at its resolution. The speaker comes to understand that human weakness and pain cannot be argued away, cannot be transcended through philosophy or escaped through longing. There is only one honest response, and it is the response that Vallejo and Johnson embodied: to sing. Not to sing sweetly in the ordinary sense, but to sing with raw and wounded intensity, to let the broken places in oneself become the very source of the music. The wound is not an obstacle to art—it is the origin of art's power.

The poem closes on this affirmation, insisting that beauty born from brokenness carries a strange and shocking sweetness, all the more vital for having passed through suffering. The art that matters is not the polished product of comfort but the cry that rises out of hurt, trembling and alive. In singing this way, the speaker suggests, we do not merely describe our fragility—we transform it, turning our deepest pain into something that can move and startle and console. This is the covenant the tormented artists made, and it is the one the speaker finally accepts as his own: to answer the ache of being human with a song wrung directly from the wound.

**The Vallejo Legacy of Robert**

In the small coastal town of Vallejo, the name Robert carried a weight that few outsiders could understand. The streets that wound through the older neighborhoods seemed to whisper his story, a tale woven into the very fabric of the community.

Robert had arrived in Vallejo decades ago, a young man with little more than ambition and a willingness to work. The city, with its industrial harbor and hardworking residents, offered him a place to build something meaningful. Over the years, he became a fixture in the community, known for his generosity and quiet determination.

The people of Vallejo remembered how Robert had transformed the local waterfront, turning a neglected stretch of shoreline into a gathering place for families. The park he helped establish still stood, its benches worn smooth by generations who came to watch the sunset over the bay.

Robert's influence extended beyond public spaces. He mentored young people, offering guidance and opportunities to those who might otherwise have been overlooked. The lessons he taught—about perseverance, kindness, and the value of hard work—rippled outward through countless lives.

When Robert passed, the entire town of Vallejo felt the loss. But his legacy endured, carried forward by all those he had touched. The story of Robert became part of Vallejo's identity, a reminder of what one dedicated person could accomplish.

Today, visitors to Vallejo might not know the full history, but they can feel it in the warmth of the community and the pride of its people. The name Robert, and the town of Vallejo, remain forever intertwined.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem that weaves together references to the poet César Vallejo and the blues musician Robert Johnson, using imagery of torn library pages, birds, and brains.
counterfactuals.output:
**Two Deaths on a Rainy Thursday**

Somebody tears a page from Vallejo
and the letters scatter like blackbirds,
the black heralds lifting off the shelf—
*I will die in Paris on a rainy day,*
he wrote, and the rain has been falling ever since
through the roof of every library
where a boy sleeps against the stacks.

Down at the crossroads Robert Johnson
tunes the storm into six strings,
a hellhound licking the salt from his shoes,
and the same rain crossing the Atlantic
to fall in the Delta, on the Seine,
on two men who both went early
with music still folded in their brains.

Their brains—little wet libraries,
gray pages God keeps thumbing through,
tearing out what He needs for the birds.
Vallejo's hunger. Johnson's crossroads.
The soft synapse where a chord
becomes a sob becomes a psalm
nobody asked to sing.

I have gathered the torn leaves
in the gutter of the stacks:
one says *there are blows in life so hard,*
one says *I got to keep movin',*
and between them a sparrow lands,
cocks its head at the ruined text,
and eats the punctuation like seed.

They were both twenty-seven, or forty-six,
or however old the rain makes you—
the wet page, the fretted neck,
the folded gray meat of a mind
that learned to bleed in a foreign key.
Somewhere a bird is stealing the last line.
Somewhere the devil retunes the strings.

Read what remains. The margin
is a levee, and it is breaking.
The heralds are black and they are landing.
The song does not resolve.
It was never meant to.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary poem exploring inner weakness and strength, artistic longing, and mortality, alluding to famous suffering artists and ending with a violent, vivid image of an apple split open.
counterfactuals.output:
# Inventory of the Soft Machine

I keep a ledger of my failures
in the same drawer as my teeth—
the ones I've lost to grinding
in the dark, jaw clenched
against the morning that arrives
regardless.

Van Gogh knew this arithmetic:
how much of yourself you spend
to buy a field of wheat that swallows crows,
how the ear you sacrifice
still hears the color yellow
screaming.

I am weak in the way water is weak,
patient against the stone,
and strong in the way water is strong—
I have not stopped
moving toward the sea
though I cannot see it.

Plath tuned her oven like a violin.
Kahlo painted her spine
a broken column, and still
the flowers bloomed
from her ruined hair.
They knew the secret:

that longing is a muscle,
that the wanting itself
is the last thing to die,
outlasting the hands
that failed to make
the beautiful thing.

I wanted to leave something
that would not rot—
a stanza, a chord, a face
rendered in oil that holds
its breath forever.
Instead I leave this:

my thumbnail pressed
against the skin of an apple,
the sudden give,
the white flesh gasping open,
seeds spilling like dark teeth,
the whole sweet wound of it
splayed and dripping
in my trembling,
mortal hand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, confessional poem in the voice of someone comparing themselves to a thrush and to tormented creative geniuses, meditating on guilt, freedom, and the desire to sing.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Thrush's Confession

I would be a thrush if I could—
that small brown throat that asks for nothing,
spilling itself at dusk across the hedges,
guiltless as rain, unburdened by the knowing.

But I am made of heavier stuff:
I carry Van Gogh's ear in my cupped hands,
the swallowed pills of every poet
who could not bear the singing's own demands.

Listen—the thrush does not apologize.
It does not weigh its song against the cost,
does not lie awake accounting for the hours
it stole from duty, or the love it lost

to make one perfect trilling in the trees.
I envy that. I envy the clean animal
that never asked permission to be free,
never mistook its hunger for a crime.

Because I want to sing. God help me, want it—
that reckless emptying, that gorgeous waste,
the way the mad ones burned their whole lives down
to leave one canvas dripping, one bright taste

of something truer than the careful life.
I hoard my voice like coins I dare not spend.
I tell myself tomorrow, tell myself
there's virtue in the holding, in the end—

but the thrush is dying even as it sings,
and knows it, maybe, in its ancient blood,
and pours the whole self out regardless, pours
until the last light drowns it like a flood.

Teach me that. Teach me to be unafraid
of my own throat, to let the guilt fall mute.
I am so tired of the unsung thing
that beats its wings against my sternum's root.

Let me be foolish. Let me be the flame.
Let me be brown and small and full of night
and open, open, open till it hurts—
and call that hurting mine. And call it flight.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem that plays with the phrase "days are dog-eared" and builds an extended metaphor about damaged books, damaged minds, and the price of art—referencing Vallejo and Johnson.
counterfactuals.output:
**Dog-Eared**

The days are dog-eared, folded down
to mark where I stopped living—
each corner creased, a promise
I would return, and never did.

Vallejo said he'd die in Paris
on a rainy day he half-remembered
forward. He was right, the way
a broken spine still knows its book,

still splays to the same abused chapter
whether you will it or not.
My mind is that abused chapter.
My mind is the water-stain

blooming through the margins,
the coffee-ring halo, the underline
pressed so hard the pencil
tore the paper it adored.

Some pages I loved to death.
That is the price: the ones you open
most are the ones that fall
first from the failing glue.

Denis Johnson knew—wrote
his damaged saints in the gray
motel-light of their skulls,
each one a folded corner

turned to say *remember this,*
each one forgetting.
The art costs what you were
before you made it: a clean copy,

unread, unhandled, whole.
I traded that. I dog-ear
everything now—the mornings,
the faces, the rain Vallejo

paid for in advance.
Fold me here. Fold me
where I stopped.
Mark the place. I won't come back,

but leave the crease—
so someone thumbing through
this ruined, softened stack of hours
will know a mind was here,

turned down against forgetting,
loving the page enough
to break it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an intense, allusive poem about wanting to escape oneself, invoking Cesar Vallejo crying and Robert Johnson's guitar, and closing with the idea that singing is better than fleeing.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Blues Knows

I would climb out through the window of my own mouth,
leave the body like a coat on the chair—
but there is Vallejo, weeping in Paris
on a Thursday that has not yet come,
his shoulders the two halves of a broken continent,
salt in the seams of every word he owns.

*I would trade this skin for weather,*
I tell the mirror that will not release me.
The self is a house with no doors,
only windows painted shut by the hands
that built me, the hands I cannot disown.

And then—that other sound.
Robert Johnson at the crossroads of the vein,
his six strings strung with a Delta lightning,
each note a hound let loose across the dark,
a bending blue that says: *there is nowhere,
there is nowhere, and still we make this noise.*

Hear me: the escape I wanted
was only ever a slower kind of dying,
the coward's algebra, subtracting the man
until the sum is nobody, is smoke.

But the guitar does not flee the hand that tears it.
Vallejo does not flee the grief—he *names* it,
lifts the whole aching weight of being
and turns it, turns it into throat.

So let me stay inside this trembling instrument.
Let me be played until I ring.
When the self grows unbearable, remember:
it is better to sing it than to run.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
